summary: (a+b)^n = Σr=0^n^nCra^n-rb^r for a positive integer n; it has n+1 terms and is proved by induction using Pascal's rule.
General term: Tr+1 = ^nCra^n-rb^r. To find a particular term, simplify the power of x in Tr+1 and equate it to the power wanted.

summary: Polar form: z = r(cosθ + isinθ) with r = |z| = √x^2+y^2 and tanθ = y/x; fix θ from the quadrant of (x, y), principal value in -π < θ ≤ π.
Multiply: moduli multiply, arguments add. Divide: moduli divide, arguments subtract.
De Moivre: left[r(cosθ+isinθ)right]^n = r^n(cos nθ + isin nθ), proved by induction for positive integers and extended to negative and rational indices.
Equating real and imaginary parts in (cosθ+isinθ)^n = cos nθ + isin nθ gives the multiple-angle formulas, e.g. cos 3θ = 4cos^3θ - 3cosθ.
n^th roots: z^1/n = r^1/nleft[cosdfracθ+2kπn + isindfracθ+2kπnright], k = 0, 1, ldots, n-1 — exactly n roots, equally spaced on a circle of radius r^1/n, forming a regular n-gon.
n^th roots of unity: 1, w, ldots, w^n-1 with w = cosdfrac2πn + isindfrac2πn; sum = 0, product = (-1)^n+1.
Cube roots of unity: 1, ω = dfrac-1+i√32, ω^2 = dfrac-1-i√32 with ω^3=1 and 1+ω+ω^2=0; reduce indices modulo 3.
Euler: e^iθ = cosθ+isinθ, z = re^iθ, e^iπ+1=0, cosθ = dfrace^iθ+e^-iθ2.

units.title: Matrix Based System of Linear Equations

sections.title: Consistency: unique solution, infinitely many, or none

summary: Every linear system is AX = B with A the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and B the column of constants.
Cramer: x = Dx/D, y = Dy/D, z = Dz/D, where D = |A| and each Dx replaces the matching column of D by B. Requires D ≠ 0.

Row-equivalent (Gauss): apply elementary row operations (Ri leftrightarrow Rj, Ri → cRi, Ri → Ri + cRj) to [A | B] until the coefficient block is upper triangular, then back substitute. Row operations never change the solution set.
Gauss-Jordan: carry on until [I | X]; the solution is the last column.
Inverse method: X = A^-1B = dfrac1|A|(adj A)B, valid only when |A| ≠ 0. Multiply on the left.
Consistency: |A| ≠ 0 → unique; |A| = 0 with a zero row in the reduced augmented matrix → infinitely many (use a parameter t); |A| = 0 with a row 0 = k ≠ 0 → no solution.
A homogeneous system has a non-trivial solution if and only if |A| = 0.

units.title: Properties of a Triangle

sections.title: Area of a triangle, and the radii R, r, r1

summary: Standard notation: a faces A, s = (a+b+c)/(2), area Δ.
Sine law: (a)/(sin A) = (b)/(sin B) = (c)/(sin C) = 2R, so a = 2Rsin A — the switch from sides to sines.
Cosine law: a^2 = b^2+c^2-2bccos A, i.e. cos A = fracb^2+c^2-a^22bc; negative cosine means an obtuse angle.
Tangent law: tan(A-B)/(2) = (a-b)/(a+b)cot(C)/(2), with (A+B)/(2) = 90^°-(C)/(2).
Projection laws: a = bcos C + ccos B, and its two cyclic partners.
Half angle laws: sin(A)/(2) = √((s-b)(s-c))/(bc), cos(A)/(2) = √(s(s-a))/(bc), tan(A)/(2) = √((s-b)(s-c))/(s(s-a)).
Area: Δ = frac12 absin C = √s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) (Heron).
Radii: R = (abc)/(4Δ), r = (Δ)/(s) = 4Rsin(A)/(2) sin(B)/(2)sin(C)/(2), r1 = (Δ)/(s-a) = stan(A)/(2), and r1+r2+r3-r = 4R.

SAS: a^2 = b^2+c^2-2bccos A; or Napier, tan(A-B)/(2) = (a-b)/(a+b)cot(C)/(2) with (A+B)/(2) = 90^°-(C)/(2).
ASA/AAS: third angle first, then (a)/(sin A) = (b)/(sin B).
SSA is ambiguous: with h = bsin A and A acute — none if a<h, one (right-angled) if a = h, two if h<a<b, one if a ≥ b.
Area: Δ = frac12 absin C = √s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c).

summary: A conic is the locus of P with PS/PM = e, where S is the focus and the directrix gives PM. e=0 circle, 0<e<1 ellipse, e=1 parabola, e>1 hyperbola. The latus rectum is the focal chord perpendicular to the axis.
Circle: (x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2; general form x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0 has centre (-g,-f) and r=√g^2+f^2-c; diameter form (x-x1)(x-x2)+(y-y1)(y-y2)=0.
A line touches a circle when the perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius; for x^2+y^2=a^2 and y=mx+c this is c^2=a^2(1+m^2), with contact point (-a^2m/c, a^2/c).
Tangent to x^2+y^2=a^2 at (x1,y1) is xx1+yy1=a^2; the normal always passes through the centre; the length of the tangent from (x1,y1) is √S1; the director circle is x^2+y^2=2a^2.
Parabola: y^2=4ax has vertex (0,0), focus (a,0), directrix x=-a, latus rectum 4a, parametric point (at^2,2at). Three sign/axis variants give the other three orientations.
Parabola tangency: y=mx+a/m touches at (a/m^2, 2a/m); the tangent at (x1,y1) is yy1=2a(x+x1); the subnormal is always 2a.
Ellipse: dfracx^2a^2+dfracy^2b^2=1 with b^2=a^2(1-e^2); foci (± ae,0), directrices x=± a/e, latus rectum 2b^2/a, and PS+PS1=2a. If b>a everything rotates onto the y-axis.
Hyperbola: dfracx^2a^2-dfracy^2b^2=1 with b^2=a^2(e^2-1); foci (± ae,0), directrices x=± a/e, latus rectum 2b^2/a, asymptotes y=± bx/a, and |PS1-PS|=2a. Rectangular when a=b, where e=√2.

summary: Scalar product: acdotb = |a||b|cosθ = a1b1+a2b2+a3b3, a number. The two forms agree by the cosine law applied to the triangle on a, b and b-a.
Angle and perpendicularity: cosθ = dfracacdotb|a||b|; for non-zero vectors aperpb Leftrightarrow acdotb = 0. Also acdota = |a|^2, icdoti = 1, icdotj = 0.
Properties of ·: commutative, distributive over addition, (ma)cdotb = m(acdotb), and |acdotb| ≤ |a||b|. You may not cancel a vector factor.
Projection: the scalar projection of b on a is dfracacdotb|a| (signed), and the vector projection is dfracacdotb|a|^2a. Work done is W = Fcdotd.

Dot-product geometry: cosine law a^2 = b^2+c^2-2bccos A; projection law a = bcos C + ccos B; cos(A± B) = cos Acos B mp sin Asin B; diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular because (a+b)·(a-b) = |a|^2-|b|^2; the angle in a semicircle is 90^°.
Vector product: atimesb = |a||b|sinθ n with n given by the right-hand rule — a vector. In components it is the 3×3 determinant with first row i,j,k, i.e. (a2b3-a3b2)i+(a3b1-a1b3)j+(a1b2-a2b1)k.
Properties of ×: anti-commutative btimesa = -(atimesb); atimesa = 0; distributive; not associative; itimesj = k round the cycle; and atimesb = 0 Leftrightarrow aparallelb for non-zero vectors.

Areas and Lagrange: |atimesb| is the area of the parallelogram on a,b; a triangle is tfrac12|ABtimesAC|; a parallelogram from its diagonals is tfrac12|d1timesd2|; and |atimesb|^2+(acdotb)^2 = |a|^2|b|^2.

summary: Correlation measures how two variables move together: positive, negative or zero; linear or curvilinear; simple, multiple or partial. The scatter diagram shows it at a glance.
Karl Pearson: r = dfracΣ dx dy√Σ dx^2Σ dy^2 (actual means), or r = dfracnΣ xy - Σ xΣ y√[nΣ x^2-(Σ x)^2][nΣ y^2-(Σ y)^2] (raw scores, or deviations from assumed means).
1 ≤ r ≤ 1; r is symmetric, unit-free and unchanged by a change of origin and scale; r = ± 1 means all points lie on a line; r = 0 means no linear relation; r^2 is the fraction of variation explained.
Spearman: rs = 1 - dfrac6Σ D^2n^3-n, with Σ D^2 replaced by Σ D^2 + Σdfracm^3-m12 when ranks are tied. Rank both variables from the same end; check Σ D = 0.
Least squares gives the normal equations Σ y = na + bΣ x and Σ xy = aΣ x + bΣ x^2, whence byx = dfracΣ dx dyΣ dx^2 and bxy = dfracΣ dx dyΣ dy^2.
The lines are y - y = byx(x - x) and x - x = bxy(y - y); both pass through (x, y).
byx = rdfracσyσx, bxy = rdfracσxσy, and r^2 = byx bxy so r = ±√byxbxy with the common sign of the two coefficients.
Predict y from x with the y-on-x line only; predict x from y with the x-on-y line only.

units.title: Probability
summary: Events are dependent when one changes the probability of the other; drawing without replacement is the standard example.
Multiplication theorem: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B mid A) = P(B)P(Amid B), and P(A∩ B∩ C) = P(A)P(Bmid A)P(Cmid A∩ B). Independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).
Conditional probability: P(A mid B) = dfracP(A∩ B)P(B), i.e. B becomes the new sample space.
On a tree diagram: multiply along a branch, add across branches; all branch probabilities from one node add to 1.
"At least one" = 1 - "none".
Total probability: P(A) = Σk P(Ek)P(A mid Ek) over a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive causes.
Bayes' theorem: P(Ei mid A) = dfracP(Ei)P(Amid Ei)Σk P(Ek)P(Amid Ek) — one branch over all the branches.
Binomial: P(X = r) = ^nCr p^rq^ n-r, mean np, variance npq.

summary: The standard derivatives, the product, quotient and chain rules, and the techniques for implicit (y gives a factor (dy)/(dx)), parametric ((dy)/(dx) = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)) and logarithmic differentiation (take ln of both sides, for u^v forms) are the working toolkit.

Hyperbolic: sinh x = frace^x-e^-x2, cosh x = frace^x+e^-x2, cosh^2x-sinh^2x=1, and (sinh x)' = cosh x, (cosh x)' = sinh x, (tanh x)' = sech^2x. Inverses: (sinh^-1x)' = frac1√x^2+1, (cosh^-1x)' = frac1√x^2-1, (tanh^-1x)' = frac11-x^2.
L'Hospital: for frac00 or (∞)/(∞) only, lim(f)/(g) = lim(f')/(g'), repeated as needed. Convert 0·∞, ∞-∞, 0^0, 1^∞ to a quotient first.
Differentials: dy = f'(x)dx and f(x+Δ x)≈ f(x) + f'(x)Δ x; relative error (dy)/(y).
Tangent at (x1,y1): y-y1 = m(x-x1) with m = f'(x1); normal: y-y1 = -(1)/(m)(x-x1).
Angle between curves: tanθ = left|(m1-m2)/(1+m1m2)right|; orthogonal if m1m2=-1.
Rates: (dy)/(dt) = (dy)/(dx)·(dx)/(dt); differentiate the relation with respect to t, then substitute. In motion, v = (ds)/(dt) and a = fracd^2sdt^2.
f' > 0 ⇒ increasing; f' < 0 ⇒ decreasing; f' = 0 ⇒ stationary.

summary: Anti-differentiation reverses differentiation: ∫ f(x) dx = F(x)+C where F' = f. The +C is compulsory, and it makes the answer a whole family of parallel curves.
Learn the table of standard integrals to the point of recall, including ∫(dx)/(x) = ln|x|, the nine quadratic forms, and ∫tan x dx = ln|sec x|, ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x+tan x|.
Substitution works when the integrand contains g(x) together with g'(x). The master pattern is ∫(g'(x))/(g(x))dx = ln|g(x)|+C.

By parts: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du, with u chosen by ILATE. Polynomial times sine or exponential needs repeated parts; e^axsin bx is cyclic, so apply parts twice and solve for I; and ∫ e^xleft[f+f'right]dx = e^xf(x)+C in one step.
A quadratic denominator is handled by completing the square; an x in the numerator by splitting px+q = λ(denominator)' + μ.
Radicals √a^2-x^2, √a^2+x^2, √x^2-a^2 call for x = asinθ, atanθ, asecθ; draw the reference triangle to convert back.
Any rational function of sin x and cos x yields to t = tan(x)/(2), using sin x = frac2t1+t^2, cos x = frac1-t^21+t^2, dx = frac2 dt1+t^2.
Rational functions: divide first if improper, then split into partial fractions according to the four denominator cases.

units.title: Differential Equations
topics: Order and degree of a differential equation
Differential equations of first order and first degree

sections.title: Order and degree of a differential equation
Differential equations of first order and first degree

summary: A differential equation relates y to its derivatives. Its order is the highest derivative present; its degree is the power of that derivative once all radicals in the derivatives have been cleared. The degree may be undefined.

The general solution of an n-th order equation contains n arbitrary constants. Extra conditions turn it into a particular solution. To form the equation of a family with n constants, differentiate n times and eliminate the constants.
A first-order first-degree equation has a one-parameter family of solutions, and the slope field is the picture of that family.
Separable: write f(y) dy = g(x) dx and integrate both sides. Test this first, because it is the cheapest method.
Homogeneous: if (dy)/(dx) = Fleft(frac yxright), put y = vx so that (dy)/(dx) = v + x(dv)/(dx). The result always separates.
Reducible to homogeneous: for (dy)/(dx) = fraca1x+b1y+c1a2x+b2y+c2, shift the origin with x = X+h, y = Y+k chosen to kill both constants.
Linear: for (dy)/(dx) + Py = Q the integrating factor is I = e^∫ P dx, and then Iy = ∫ IQ dx + C.
Exact: M dx + N dy = 0 is exact when (partial M)/(partial y) = (partial N)/(partial x), and the solution is u = C where (partial u)/(partial x) = M and (partial u)/(partial y) = N.

summary: Gauss elimination. Form [A | b]; use Ri → Ri - mikRk with mik = aik/akk to make it upper triangular; back substitute. Swap rows if a pivot is 0 (partial pivoting).
A row 0;0;0 | k with k ≠ 0 means no solution; 0;0;0 | 0 means infinitely many.

Gauss–Seidel. x^(k+1) = frac1a11(b1 - a12y^(k) - a13z^(k)), and so on, always using the newest value available. Converges for certain when |aii| > Σj≠ i|aij| in every row — reorder the equations if it is not so.
Direct methods (elimination) finish in a set number of steps; iterative methods (Gauss–Seidel) are stopped when successive iterates agree to the required accuracy.
LPP. Maximise Z = c1x + c2y over a convex feasible region; the optimum lies at a corner.

Simplex. Add slacks, write Z - c1x - c2y = 0. Pivot column = most negative Z entry; pivot row = smallest positive ratio RHS ÷ column entry; pivot to make the column (1,0,ldots,0). Stop when no Z entry is negative.
Newton–Raphson. xn+1 = xn - f(xn)/f'(xn); correct digits roughly double each step.
Quadrature. Trapezium (h)/(2)[y0+yn+2(rest)] with |E| ≤ ((b-a)h^2)/(12)max|f''|; Simpson (h)/(3)[y0+yn+4(odd)+2(even)], n even, with |E| ≤ ((b-a)h^4)/(180)max|f^(4)|.

summary: Resultant of P and Q at angle θ: R = √P^2+Q^2+2PQcosθ, at tanα = dfracQsinθP+Qcosθ to P. Resolution: components Fcosθ, Fsinθ.
Triangle law. Three concurrent forces are in equilibrium exactly when they form a closed head-to-tail triangle; with more forces, a closed polygon.
Lami's theorem. For three concurrent forces in equilibrium, dfracPsinα = dfracQsinβ = dfracRsinγ, each angle being between the other two forces.
Moment M = F× d; a rigid body is in equilibrium when Σ Fx = 0, Σ Fy = 0 and Σ M = 0.
Newton's laws. F = ma; impulse FΔ t = mv - mu; momentum m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2 is conserved in every collision.
Atwood machine: a = dfrac(m1-m2)gm1+m2, T = dfrac2m1m2gm1+m2. Lift: R = m(g ± a).
Work W = Fscosθ; work–energy theorem W = tfrac12 mv^2 - tfrac12 mu^2; power P = Fv.

summary: A binary operation on G assigns to each ordered pair (a, b) a unique element a * b of G; the closure requirement is part of the definition.
(G, ) is a group if it is closed, associative, has an identity e and every element has an inverse; it is abelian if ab = b*a for all a, b, and the order |G| is the number of elements.
The Cayley table shows closure (all entries in G), the identity (a row repeating the heading), inverses (one e in each row and column) and the abelian property (symmetry about the leading diagonal).
Standard examples: (mathbbZ, +) infinite abelian; (Z4, +4) and 1, -1, i, -i under × finite abelian of order 4; (1,2,3,4 ×5) abelian of order 4; S3 non-abelian of order 6.
In any group the identity and each inverse are unique.
Rolle's theorem. f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) and f(a) = f(b) ⇒ there is c ∈ (a,b) with f'(c) = 0.

Mean Value Theorem. f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) ⇒ there is c ∈ (a,b) with f'(c) = dfracf(b)-f(a)b-a; it follows from Rolle applied to g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a)(x-a).
Trapezoidal rule dfrach2[(y0+yn) + 2(interior)] with |ET| ≤ dfrac(b-a)h^212max|f''|; Simpson's rule (n even) dfrach3[(y0+yn) + 4(odd) + 2(even)] with |ES| ≤ dfrac(b-a)h^4180max|f^(4)|.
